newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cash-strapped Pakistan said seeking foreign loans.
newsitem.headline: Cash-strapped Pakistan said seeking foreign loans.

text.p: Pakistan, faced with heavy debt repayments in October-December, is trying to raise money from international markets, analysts said on Wednesday.

They said falling reserves, a gaping trade deficit and the International Monetary Fund's reluctance to resume payments of a $600 million standby loan had forced the government to seek expensive short-term loans to meet debt servicing commitments.
Such reliance on short- and medium-term commercial borrowing could itself worsen the current account position by adding to an already onerous debt service burden, they said.
"Pakistan is facing a difficult situation and its forex reserves position is a cause of concern," Farrukh Hasan, country head of Crosby Securities, told Reuters.
The State (central) Bank of Pakistan said foreign exchange reserves stood at $831 million, excluding bullion, on October 3.
"Pakistan is currently negotiating with a U.S.-based securities firm to arrange a $100 million floating rate note (FRN) issue," Hasan said. He did not identify the firm.
Pakistan issued a $150 million FRN in June at 200 basis points above the London Interbank Offered Rate.

Hasan said any new issue would cost Pakistan more because of a higher risk following last month's move by the U.S. agency Moody's Investor Service Inc to place Pakistani credit ratings under review for possible downgrading.
A foreign banker, who asked not to be named, said Pakistan needed to pay about $700 million in debt repayments this quarter.
"If we assume that Pakistan will have an inflow equal to that in the same period last year, the government will still have to tide over a net outflow of $450 million," he said.
He said some foreign banks had told the central bank they would roll over existing loans of more than $300 million on condition the government did not deduct a 58 percent witholding tax.
Hasan said Pakistan had approached some Middle East-based banks for a $100 million short-term loan, while state-run Sui Northern Gas and Pakistan State Oil were also seeking loans.
"It seems the government is trying to snap up dollars from any source and at any price they can get at present," he said.
Analysts said Pakistan's foreign debt servicing bill was likely to reach $4 billion in 1996/97 (July-June), or more than 30 percent of foreign exchange earnings.

Analyst Sakib Sherani of Smith International Securities said in a research report that Pakistan's total external debt reached a provisional $24.4 billion at the end of 1994/95, equivalent to 40 percent of gross domestic product at market prices.
He said payments on short- and medium-term commercial debt had risen 430 percent since 1991/92 to $1.37 billion in 1994/95.

Official figures show that Pakistan's trade gap rose to a provisional $276 million in September from $219 million in August. "With the latest figures showing a rising import trend, Pakistan is in dire need of IMF assistance," Hasan said.
Pakistani officials are now in Washington holding talks with the IMF on an economic rescue package that would meet the fund's conditions for renewed disbursements of the standby loan.
